title: Hillslope-scale daily snow cover reconstruction in complex mountains: a novel framework integrating long-term snow persistence
A semi-empirical BPDF model for improving characterization of polarimetric reflection of land surfaces: Validation using laboratory and POLDER polarization data
abstract: Bidirectional Polarization Distribution Function (BPDF) models, widely used to characterize the polarimetric properties of light reflected from targets, are crucial for linking polarization with land surface structural parameters and understanding surface contributions to polarization in radiative transfer. However, existing BPDF models face challenges in accurately representing variations in both the magnitude and distribution of polarimetric reflection across surfaces with varying structural characteristics. In this study, a three-parameter BPDF model (GMF model), which can effectively characterize polarimetric reflection of surfaces ranging from smooth to rough, was developed by combining the GGX distribution function with the Fresnel equation and a shadowing function. Multi-angular polarimetric data from laboratory measurements over three plant samples and from Polarization and Directionality of the Earth's Reflectances (POLDER) satellite observations over various land surfaces, each exhibiting distinct polarimetric reflection properties, were used to validate the proposed model. Compared with five existing models, the new model achieved the highest accuracy in simulating polarimetric reflection, reducing the overall RMSE by 33%–68% for laboratory samples and by 8%–30% for POLDER observations. This improvement is attributed to the incorporation of the GGX distribution function, which enables the new polarization model to accurately characterize the polarimetric properties of surfaces with varying structures, including sharp specular peaks over smooth surfaces and broad angular distributions over rough surfaces. Furthermore, the analysis of the model's response to parameter variations demonstrated that the GGX distribution function enhanced the ability of the GMF model to modulate the magnitude and distribution of polarimetric reflection induced by surface structure variations. The proposed polarization model is expected to advance polarized remote sensing applications in land surface monitoring.

title: Extent and dynamics of tropical flooded forests with multi-year SAR composites and altimetry
abstract: Flood dynamics regulate greenhouse gas emissions from tropical flooded forests, but monitoring flooding beneath dense canopies is challenging. We introduce a L-band SAR approach that uses more than a decade of ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 observations to detect sub-canopy flooding at 100 m resolution across the Amazon and Congo rainforests. We generate multi-year composites of HH and HV backscatter that represent low-, intermediate-, and high-water stages. These hydrological stages are defined locally using over 7000 satellite altimetry time series, accounting for the large variability in the timings of high-water conditions across both rainforests. Flooded forests display a characteristic dual-polarization signature: HV backscatter is comparable to that of non-flooded forests, while HH backscatter is higher due to double-bounce scattering. Quantifying deviations in the HH-HV space, we determine the extent of flooded forests at high-water stage and estimate their seasonal dynamics using a discrete stage-count metric, informing on the number of hydrological stages at which a pixel is classified as flooded forest. Multi-year compositing reduces speckle noise relative to single scenes, enabling the detection of narrow floodplains, while the local definition of high-water conditions improves the representation of high-water conditions across the two rainforests. We estimate approximately 827,000 km 2 of flooded forests under typical high-water conditions, ~687,000 km 2 in the Amazon and ~ 140,000 km 2 in the Congo rainforest. In the Amazon basin, agreement with estimates from Hess et al. (2015), Rosenqvist et al. (2020) and Fleischmann et al. (2022) varies spatially, with high agreement in wide floodplains (e.g., Solimões and Purus rivers), lower agreement along narrower floodplains, and substantial discrepancies in sparsely vegetated areas, partly explained by differences in forest definitions. In the Cuvette Centrale, our estimates show spatial consistency with the estimated extent of peat swamp forests by Crezee et al. (2022), although our flooded forest extent is more spatially restricted. We also found a good correlation between our stage-count map and the microtopography of the Solimões floodplain. By resolving both the extent and seasonal dynamics of flooded forests at 100 m resolution, these maps can support ecological, hydrological, and carbon studies in tropical forests.

title: Quantile-based homogeneity selection and similarity-weighted robust coherence matrix for distributed scatterer interferometry in mining deformation monitoring
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Coal mining can lead to a series of geological issues, making it crucial to monitor surface deformation for early hazard warning in mining areas. Distributed Scatterer Interferometry (DSI) enables the monitoring of deformation in overlying strata above mining working faces. However, the accuracy of this technology is often affected by spatiotemporal decorrelation, necessitating phase recovery processing. The Phase Linking (PL) algorithm can effectively recover the interferometric phase, but it is limited by the correctness of statistical homogeneous pixel selection (SHPs) and the utilization of spatial dimensional information, making it difficult to obtain a sample complex coherence matrix (SCCM) that closely resembles the true situation. This severely impacts the accuracy of the PL estimation results. To address this, this paper proposes two solutions: (1) For SHPs, the medcouple (MC) method is used as a robust measure of skewed distributions, adjusting the boxplot to optimize homogeneous samples in the intensity map, removing outliers and enhancing sample robustness; (2) For SCCM construction, a similarity measure between reference pixels and homogeneous pixels is used as a weight, and a weighted sum with constraint processing is applied to obtain a robust coherence matrix. Simulation and real-world results show that the proposed method can recover phase information severely affected by noise, maintain phase stability, and significantly increase the monitoring point density; its high reliability has been validated through leveling data verification.

title: Design for Machinability: Topology Optimization for Subtractive Machining Using Trimmed Neural Fields
abstract: Topology optimization has found significant utility in additive manufacturing, but the resulting geometries are often difficult to realize using subtractive methods. The complex, curved surfaces of optimized designs typically require time-consuming point milling operations. In contrast, geometries composed of developable surfaces are well suited to flank milling, enabling substantial improvements in machining efficiency and surface quality. However, globally minimizing Gaussian curvature leads to overly simplistic designs. We address this challenge with a novel method that represents geometry using three implicit neural fields, optimized to produce machinable components. The resulting designs consist of regions of developable surfaces separated by seamlines where curvature is concentrated. Seamlines are efficiently computed as intersections of the implicit fields, while the geometry emerges through their product. By constraining surfaces to align with the cutter’s normal or tangential direction, our approach further accommodates practical constraints of 3-axis machining. We demonstrate concurrent optimization of topology and Gaussian curvature, enabling control over seamline feature scale. Compared to methods that enforce subtractive machinability without considering milling efficiency, our approach consistently reduces machining time while maintaining competitive structural performance.

title: Methodology for assessing the accuracy of long-term, annual land cover monitoring at national scale: Experiences from the Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) initiative
abstract: Annual land cover monitoring using medium-resolution satellite imagery represents a transition from periodic mapping campaigns to continuous observation systems. This transition introduces accuracy assessment challenges not encountered in one-time mapping efforts, particularly when the initial monitoring period is extended forward in time. These challenges are not addressed in existing guidance, which remains largely framed around the evaluation of maps of a single date or maps showing changes between two dates. We present a set of methodological adaptations to adjust to this evolving paradigm, using as a case study the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) initiative, which generated annual land cover and land cover change products across the historical Landsat archive. Assessing the accuracy of these products was an essential component of LCMAP and resulted in an extensive reference sample dataset that may be used for accuracy estimation, area estimation, or support in the development of new algorithms or models. We review the LCMAP methodology and highlight challenges encountered and lessons learned that are transferable to other long-term, temporally dense monitoring programs. This framework demonstrates that statistically rigorous assessment can scale to operational annual land cover production, while the experiences of the project clarify where existing good practice guidance should be extended to support the needs of ongoing, continuous land cover monitoring.
